description: We are a motivated and creative team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are passionate about space exploration, technology, and discovering new ways to understand Mars. For the Martian Mapping Challenge, we aim to turn scientific data into meaningful maps and innovative solutions. We welcome team members with skills in programming, GIS, data analysis, planetary science, and design. Most importantly, we value creativity, teamwork, curiosity, and a willingness to learn.
summary: Navimartian is a route planner for a Mars rover. It stacks NASA Mars Trek imagery and Mars Global Surveyor MOLA topography at five real sites, then searches three corridors for a pressurized rover: the lowest radiation dose, the shortest travel time, and a custom balance of slope, radiation, and dust. Each corridor reports distance, time, dose, oxygen, battery energy, and a point-by-point safety score. A local dust storm and a solar particle event update the route without rewriting the terrain file. Github page: https://github.com/teamwasp2/Navimartian
details:
Navimartian answers the Martian Map challenge with one working view of a route. A crew can pick Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Valles Marineris, Arcadia Planitia, or the Olympus Mons summit, set a start and a destination on the terrain, and compare three ways to walk it.

The map has three layers from NASA Mars Trek. The color drape is the Viking MDIM 2.1 global mosaic. Relief shading is the MOLA and Mars Express HRSC blend. Elevation is the 463 m MOLA grayscale DEM, read at Trek zoom 5, stretched onto that site’s elevation envelope, and smoothed so the coarse grid does not stair-step. Slope is then recomputed from the real east-west and north-south ground spacing. The vertical-exaggeration slider only stretches the picture. Grade percent stays the true rise over run. Mars radius in that spacing is 3,389.5 km.

The search is eight-connected A*. Safest minimizes cumulative dose, with a tiny along-track grade tie-break. Fastest minimizes 3D travel time. Custom multiplies meters by the slope, radiation, and dust weights on the sliders. Cells steeper than the slope limit are impassable. Heavy Cargo uses a 15% limit. Light Scout uses 25% and weights radiation more heavily. A diagonal step cannot cut a corner through a blocked cell.

Traverse time, battery, and oxygen come from a pressurized-rover force balance at 3.72 m/s² and 2,500 kg, on the scale of NASA’s Space Exploration Vehicle concept. Rolling resistance rises with the dust field. The drivetrain is 82% efficient, downhill regeneration returns 35%, and the cabin draws 1.8 kW. Flat speed is 2.4 m/s, reduced by dust slip, and capped by a 10 kW traction bus when the grade demands it. Dose on a step is the average of the two cells’ rates, times hours, divided by 24.

The background radiation field is anchored to Curiosity RAD at Gale: 0.64 mSv/day during the first 300 sols, from Hassler and colleagues (2014). Thinner air raises the rate on an 11.1 km scale height. A solar particle event adds 2.8 mSv/day at the highest cell and less below it. A dust storm is a hard disk 22 cells across. Both hazards can be on together, and neither one edits the terrain file. If either appears while the rover is moving, both corridors replan from the last cell reached.

The safety score is a display index, shown to one decimal, with separate penalties for radiation rate, accumulated dose, average grade, dust, the steepest cell, and time. It is not the quantity the search minimizes. The in-app Bibliography marks every measurement, data product, method, and planner choice, including the rolling-resistance equation and the 2.8 mSv/day surge, so those choices are not presented as NASA measurements.

On Jezero, with no storm, the three corridors are each 22.83 km. Safest takes 3.06 h and 0.081 mSv, safety 76.0, on 1.4% average grade. Fastest takes 2.99 h and 0.091 mSv, safety 69.4, on 4.9% average grade. The lines split by up to 0.7 km. Export writes a JSON mission plan with the site, the hazards, the three corridors, and latitude and longitude waypoints.
dataRefs: NASA Mars Trek, Jet Propulsion Laboratory and NASA Ames. Equirectangular WMTS used for every site.
Viking Orbiter MDIM 2.1 color mosaic, 232 m, recolored by NASA Ames and published by the USGS Astrogeology Science Center. Trek layer Mars_Viking_MDIM21_ClrMosaic_global_232m, zoom 7.
Mars Global Surveyor MOLA elevation mosaic, 463 m. Trek layer Mars_MGS_MOLA_DEM_mosaic_global_463m_8, zoom 5.
NASA Mars Fact Sheet, for the 3,389.5 km volumetric mean radius and the gravity and scale-height context.
NASA Space Exploration Vehicle fact sheet, for the vehicle class.

MOLA and ESA Mars Express HRSC shaded relief. Trek layer Mars_MOLA_blend200ppx_HRSC_Shade_clon0dd_200mpp_lzw, zoom 8. HRSC is described in Neukum and Jaumann, ESA SP-1240 (2004), and Gwinner and colleagues, Planetary and Space Science (2016)
Curiosity RAD surface dose, the 0.64 mSv/day Gale anchor. Hassler and colleagues, Science (2014)
